summary: payment-service error rate jumped from ~0.2% to ~61% at 15:00, with "ledger write failed: No space left on device". The fault does NOT originate in payment-service: the shared ledger-db (postgres) filled its disk from WAL retained by an inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc'. Disk on ledger-db climbed monotonically 89% (13:00) → 100% (~14:45), before the 14:46 v6.0.0 deploy; the first write failures at 15:00 hit every service on ledger-db — payment-service AND order-service (a different team with no deploy) simultaneously. Rolling back v6.0.0 at 15:12 did not reduce the error rate (still ~61-63% through 16:59). Root cause is resource_exhaustion at ledger-db caused by the orphaned replication slot; the v6.0.0 deployment is coincidental timing.

ranked_hypotheses.title: ledger-db disk exhaustion from orphaned replication slot (resource_exhaustion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: An inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' on the shared ledger-db retained WAL until the data volume reached 100% full; once full, all writers to ledger-db (payment-service, order-service, etc.) failed with 'No space left on device', surfacing as payment-service 61% error rate.

causal_chain.claim: Orphaned replication slot 'analytics_cdc' accumulates WAL on ledger-db
WAL accumulation drives disk_used_pct from 89% to 100% by ~14:45, before any deploy
Disk full causes all ledger-db writes to fail at 15:00 (PANIC / could not extend file)
Shared-datastore failure propagates to every caller: payment-service AND order-service fail simultaneously
Rollback of the unrelated payment deploy does not help because disk remains full

assumptions: The 'analytics_cdc' slot is genuinely orphaned/inactive and not a required consumer
WAL retention is the dominant disk consumer (slot MBs are large and consistent with filling the volume)

ranked_hypotheses.title: payment-service v6.0.0 introduced a bad ledger write path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The new MANDATE_HOLD ledger entry type in v6.0.0 caused malformed/failed ledger writes, producing the error surge.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Errors are disk-full ('No space left on device'), not code/schema errors; disk was already 100% before the 14:46 deploy; the unrelated order-service failed identically at the same minute; the rollback at 15:12 did not reduce the error rate.

facts.statement: Error onset was 15:00; payment-service error_rate jumped from ~0.2% to ~61% at the 15:00 bucket.
All payment-service errors were ledger writes failing with 'No space left on device' (first at 15:00:26).
ledger-db disk usage reached 100% by ~14:45, before the 14:46 deploy, and stayed full.
An inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' was retaining tens of GB of WAL since at least 13:02.
ledger-db logged PANIC/file-extend 'No space left on device' errors from 15:01:01.
order-service, an unrelated team with no deploy, failed with 'No space left on device' from 15:00:42.
ledger-db is a shared DB used by order, portfolio, payment and settlement services.
The 15:12 rollback of v6.0.0 did not reduce payment-service error rate.
payment-service local memory and DB pool metrics were flat, ruling out local exhaustion.
Historical incident HIST-114 matched this exact pattern (inactive slot WAL filling ledger-db disk).

assumptions: The 'analytics_cdc' replication slot is orphaned and safe to drop after confirming no active CDC consumer
WAL retention from the slot is the dominant contributor to the disk growth
No other disk consumer (e.g. table bloat) materially contributed

timeline.event: ledger-db begins warning: inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' retaining WAL (33GB, peaking ~92GB)
payment-service v6.0.0 (dep-6203) deployed — coincidental, disk already full
payment-service first 'ledger write failed: No space left on device'
order-service also fails with 'No space left on device'
ledger-db PANIC writing pg_wal — disk exhausted
payment-service v6.0.0 rolled back; error rate unchanged

recommended_actions.action: Free space on ledger-db: drop/invalidate the inactive 'analytics_cdc' replication slot and let WAL reclaim (after confirming no active consumer).
recommended_actions.rationale: The orphaned slot is retaining tens of GB of WAL, keeping the volume at 100% and blocking all writes.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT treat the v6.0.0 rollback as the fix; rollback is already shown not to help. Re-deploy or keep v6.0.0 as appropriate once disk is restored.
recommended_actions.rationale: Error rate did not change after the 15:12 rollback; the deploy is coincidental.

recommended_actions.action: Add alerting on replication-slot WAL retention / slot inactivity and on ledger-db disk_used_pct above threshold.
recommended_actions.rationale: HIST-114 resolution already called for a slot-lag alert; recurrence suggests it was not adequately covered.

recommended_actions.action: Audit and cap replication slot WAL retention (max_slot_wal_keep_size) and add a watchdog that invalidates slots inactive beyond a limit.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents a single orphaned slot from filling the shared datastore again.

data_gaps: Whether the 'analytics_cdc' slot has a legitimate active consumer cannot be confirmed from available telemetry (bank-partner-api and vendor systems have no telemetry; no slot-consumer visibility).
portfolio-service and settlement-service produced no errors in the window despite sharing ledger-db — possibly write frequency or cache differences, not fully explained.
No explicit post-fix recovery datapoint (disk still 100% at end of window); causal chain is confirmed by mechanism but the resolution has not been observed.

findings.statement: payment-service error_rate was ~0.2% until 14:45, then jumped to 61.02% in the 15:00 bucket and stayed ~61-63% through 16:45.
The only change in the window was deployment dep-6203 of payment-service v6.0.0 at 14:46 ('New UPI mandate flow', new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD), rolled back at 15:12.
No config or feature-flag changes occurred in the window.
payment-service errors are all 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device', first seen 15:00:26.

refs.quote: ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device (payment e3489438)

findings.statement: ledger-db disk_used_pct rose monotonically from 89.18% at 13:00 to 100% by ~14:45 and stayed at 100% through 16:45 — i.e. the disk was already full before/at the 14:46 deploy.
ledger-db reported an inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' retaining tens of GB of WAL starting 13:02:25 (e.g. 92599 MB) and repeated warnings through 14:49:47.

refs.quote: replication slot 'analytics_cdc' is inactive; retaining 92599 MB of WAL

findings.statement: ledger-db logged PANIC / could-not-extend-file 'No space left on device' errors (153 pg_wal/xlogtemp panics, 139 file extend errors) beginning 15:01:01.

refs.quote: PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.37478": No space left on device

findings.statement: order-service — a different team with no deployment in the window — also began failing at 15:00:42 with 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device' (236 errors).

refs.quote: INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device orderId=8ab6dc3a

findings.statement: ledger-db is a shared datastore used by order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service.
The rollback of v6.0.0 at 15:12 did not restore service: payment-service error_rate remained ~61-63% for the rest of the window (last bucket 16:45 avg 62.49).
payment-service memory_pct (≈55%) and db_pool_in_use (≈8) were flat across the window, ruling out local resource exhaustion in payment-service.
ledger-db replication_lag_ms rose steadily from ~2468ms (13:00) to ~5226ms (16:45), indicating a lagging/unconsumed replication stream.
Historical incident HIST-114 (2025-04-18) on ledger-db had the identical pattern: 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled', category resource_exhaustion.

refs.quote: Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled

findings.statement: ledger-db connections_active stayed flat ~62 before and after onset, ruling out connection-pool exhaustion.
